questions.question: What is @InjectMocks in Mockito and how does it work?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Mockito Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @InjectMocks creates an instance of the class under test and automatically injects @Mock and @Spy dependencies into it. It tries constructor injection first, then setter injection, then field injection. This eliminates manual instantiation like new OrderService(mockRepo, mockEmail) in every test method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of Mockito test setup automation and the three-phase dependency injection strategy it uses
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) which enables the annotation processing, or not understanding that injection silently fails if no matching strategy works
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three-phase injection strategy with priority order and the silent failure gotcha—if injection fails, @InjectMocks creates the object with null dependencies causing NullPointerExceptions

sections.title: How @InjectMocks Automates Test Setup
sections.content:
Writing unit tests for Spring services means your class under test has dependencies—repositories, other services, validators. Without **@InjectMocks**, you'd manually wire them in every test: new OrderService(mockRepo, mockEmailService, mockValidator). That's tedious and error-prone. @InjectMocks tells Mockito "create an instance of this class and inject all the @Mock and @Spy fields into it automatically." It's like Spring's @Autowired but for tests. Mockito tries three strategies in order: **constructor injection** (preferred, calls the constructor with mocks as arguments), then **setter injection** (calls setXxx methods), then **field injection** (uses reflection to set private fields directly).

Think of it like a locksmith trying three different keys. If all three fail, Mockito doesn't throw an error—it creates the object anyway with null dependencies, which causes NullPointerException when your test runs. You must also annotate your test class with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to activate annotation processing. Without it, @InjectMocks does nothing and your class field stays null.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|InjectMocks|~Builds the subject|collects Mock fields|injects automatically|constructor preferred
blue|How It Picks|~Order matters|constructor, setter, field|by type then name|silent on failure
emerald|Gotcha|~Null dependencies|when no match|prefer constructor|or wire by hand

sections.title: InjectMocks with Constructor Injection
When to Use @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Use **@InjectMocks** in every unit test for service classes with multiple dependencies. It eliminates boilerplate setup code and makes tests cleaner. This is standard for testing Spring services annotated with @Service or @Component.

Use constructor injection in your production code (the preferred Spring pattern) and @InjectMocks will match it automatically.

Avoid @InjectMocks when your class has complex initialization logic beyond dependency injection—like builders, factory methods, or constructor parameters that aren't dependencies. In those cases, manually instantiate with new and pass mocks explicitly. Also skip it when writing integration tests with @SpringBootTest, where Spring's real context should handle injection. @InjectMocks is purely for isolated unit tests with Mockito.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Without this annotation on the test class, Mockito's annotation processing never runs. Your @Mock fields become null, and @InjectMocks doesn't create the object, causing NullPointerException on the first line of your test. Always pair these two annotations.
- **Silent injection failure**: If your class has no matching constructor, no setters, and private final fields, all three injection strategies fail. Mockito creates the object anyway with null dependencies. Your test compiles but crashes at runtime. Enable Mockito's strict mode or write a setup assertion checking dependencies aren't null.
- **Mixing @InjectMocks with manual instantiation**: Writing @InjectMocks private OrderService service = new OrderService(...) defeats the purpose. Remove the = new part and let Mockito handle it entirely.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@InjectMocks**: creates an instance of the class under test and automatically injects all @Mock and @Spy dependencies
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: required on test class to activate Mockito's annotation processing, without it @InjectMocks does nothing
- **Three-phase injection**: tries constructor injection first (preferred), then setter injection, then field injection using reflection
- **Constructor injection priority**: Mockito prefers constructors because they enforce required dependencies at compile time, matching Spring's best practice
- **Silent failure risk**: if all three injection strategies fail, Mockito creates the object with null dependencies causing runtime NullPointerException
- **Field assignment prohibited**: don't write @InjectMocks private Service service = new Service() because it prevents Mockito from controlling instantiation
- **Scope limitation**: use only for isolated unit tests with Mockito, not integration tests where Spring context should handle injection

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-InjectMocks is a Mockito annotation that creates an instance of your class under test and automatically injects all the at-Mock and at-Spy dependencies into it. So instead of writing new OrderService with all the mocks in parentheses in every test method, you just annotate the field with at-InjectMocks and Mockito does it for you. Here's how it works. Mockito tries three injection strategies in order. First, it looks for a constructor that matches your mock types and calls it—that's constructor injection and it's the preferred way. If there's no matching constructor, it tries calling setter methods like setRepository. If that fails, it uses reflection to directly assign values to private fields. That's field injection. The gotcha is if all three strategies fail, Mockito doesn't throw an error. It still creates the object but leaves dependencies as null. Then your test crashes with NullPointerException when it tries to use them. The mistake freshers make is forgetting to put at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class on the test class. Without that, Mockito's annotation processing never runs. Your at-Mock fields stay null and at-InjectMocks doesn't create anything. You'll see NullPointerException on the first line of your test and wonder why. So always pair those two annotations together. Another tip—write your service classes with constructor injection for dependencies. That's Spring's best practice anyway, and it makes at-InjectMocks work cleanly because constructor injection is Mockito's first choice.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @Spy in Mockito?
questions.title: @Mock vs @Spy Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @Mock creates a fully fake object where all methods return default values (null, 0, false) unless stubbed. @Spy wraps a real object instance where unstubbed methods call the real implementation; only configured methods are overridden. Use @Spy when you need partial mocking of a real object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's core annotation differences and when to apply each in real test scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Spy everywhere thinking it's safer, or using @Mock when you actually need some real behavior to execute
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Spy is particularly useful for testing legacy services where you want real logic but need to intercept specific external calls like database queries

sections.title: Understanding Mock vs Spy in Mockito
sections.content:
When writing unit tests for Spring services, you need to isolate your class from its dependencies. **@Mock** creates a completely hollow shell—a fake object where every method returns Java's default values (null for objects, 0 for numbers, false for booleans) unless you explicitly tell it what to return.

Think of it like a mannequin in a store: it looks like a person but does nothing on its own. **@Spy**, on the other hand, is a real object wrapped in Mockito's recording layer. It's like having your actual teammate do their job, but you can tap them on the shoulder and say "for this one task, do it my way instead." Unstubbed methods execute the real code. Use @Mock when you don't want any real logic running—just fake responses. Use @Spy when the real implementation is mostly correct but you need to override specific methods like database calls or HTTP requests during testing.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the Mock annotation|~A full fake|all methods stubbed|return defaults|no real code runs
blue|the Spy annotation|~A real object wrapped|real methods run|stub selectively|a partial mock
emerald|Spy Gotcha|~Use do return|when calls the real method|side effects fire|prefer mock if unsure

sections.title: Mock vs Spy Behavior Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Mock | @Spy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Object Creation | Fully fake hollow object | Wraps real object instance |
| Unstubbed Method Behavior | Returns null/0/false defaults | Executes real method implementation |
| Stubbing Requirement | Must stub every needed method | Only stub methods you want overridden |
| Use Case | Complete isolation from dependencies | Partial mocking of real objects |
| Performance | Fastest—no real code runs | Slower—real code executes for unstubbed methods |

sections.title: Mock and Spy in Action
Choosing Between Mock and Spy
sections.content:
Use **@Mock** when testing business logic that depends on external systems like databases, REST clients, or message queues—you want zero real interaction. For example, testing OrderService that calls OrderRepository should mock the repository so no database queries run.

Use **@Spy** when working with utility classes or legacy services where most logic is correct but you need to fake specific slow or flaky methods. If you're testing a PaymentService that validates card numbers (fast, no side effects) but also calls a third-party fraud API (slow, unreliable), spy the service and stub only the fraud check method. Another common case: testing a class with private helper methods you want to keep real while faking only the collaborators.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Spy as default**: Freshers think spies are safer because they run real code, but this defeats unit testing's isolation purpose. If your spy's real methods call databases or external APIs, your tests become slow integration tests. Always prefer @Mock for external dependencies.
- **Forgetting to initialize @Spy with an instance**: Writing @Spy private EmailValidator validator; without = new EmailValidator() causes NullPointerException. @Spy requires an actual object to wrap.
- **Mixing when().thenReturn() with @Spy**: Using when(spy.method()) accidentally invokes the real method during stubbing. Always use doReturn().when(spy).method() for spies to avoid unwanted execution during test setup.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Mock**: creates empty shell object returning default values (null, 0, false) for all methods unless stubbed
- **@Spy**: wraps real object instance where unstubbed methods execute actual implementation code
- **Stubbing requirement**: mocks need explicit stubbing for every call; spies only need stubs for overridden behavior
- **Isolation principle**: prefer @Mock for dependencies to keep tests fast and isolated from external systems
- **Partial mocking**: use @Spy when you need most real behavior but must fake specific expensive operations
- **Initialization**: @Spy must be assigned an object instance (= new Class()) or Mockito creates broken wrapper
- **Syntax safety**: always use doReturn().when(spy) instead of when(spy).thenReturn() to avoid invoking real methods during setup

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd say at-Mock creates a completely fake object where every method returns default values like null or zero unless you stub it. It's like a hollow shell. At-Spy is different—it wraps a real object, so unstubbed methods actually run the real code. You only stub the methods you want to override. Here's when you'd use each. If you're testing an OrderService that talks to a database repository, you'd mock the repository because you don't want real database calls in unit tests. The mock gives you full control—you tell it exactly what to return. But let's say you have a PaymentService with ten methods, nine of them are simple calculations, and only one calls an external fraud detection API. You'd spy the PaymentService so the nine calculation methods run normally, and you'd stub only that one slow API call. The common mistake freshers make is using spy everywhere thinking it's safer because it runs real code. But that defeats the purpose of unit testing. You end up with slow tests that hit real systems. Another gotcha is forgetting to initialize the spy with an actual object—at-Spy needs something real to wrap, like at-Spy private EmailValidator validator equals new EmailValidator. Without that, you get null pointer exceptions. So the rule of thumb: mock your dependencies for isolation, spy only when you need partial mocking of the class under test itself.

questions.question: What is a test double and what are the different types?
questions.title: Test Double Types | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Test doubles are fake objects that replace real dependencies in unit tests to provide isolation. The five types are Dummy (unused placeholder), Stub (returns canned data), Fake (simplified working implementation), Mock (records and verifies calls), and Spy (wraps real object with selective stubbing).

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise vocabulary around test doubles and understanding that mock is not a catch-all term for all test replacements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling everything a mock when they're actually using stubs or fakes, showing imprecise thinking about testing strategy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Gerard Meszaros who defined these terms in xUnit Test Patterns, and map each type to its Mockito or Spring Test equivalent with concrete examples

sections.title: The Five Types of Test Doubles
sections.content:
In unit testing, a **test double** is any object that stands in for a real dependency—like a stunt double in movies. Gerard Meszaros formalized five distinct types in his book xUnit Test Patterns, and understanding these prevents sloppy thinking where developers call everything a "mock." Think of test doubles like movie production roles: a **Dummy** is an extra in the background—present but never used.

A **Stub** is a scripted actor who always delivers the same lines (canned responses). A **Fake** is a professional stunt performer who actually does simplified versions of the real action. A **Mock** is a director's assistant who records every take and verifies actors hit their marks. A **Spy** is a method actor who improvises most scenes but follows the script for key moments. Each serves a different testing purpose. Dummies fill parameter lists. Stubs provide predictable data. Fakes give lightweight working implementations. Mocks verify interactions happened. Spies wrap real objects with selective overrides. Using precise terminology shows you understand testing strategy, not just tool syntax.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Test Double|~Umbrella term|any fake stand-in|five sub-types|the Meszaros taxonomy
blue|The Types|~Each has a role|dummy, stub, fake|spy and mock|mock verifies
emerald|In Mockito|~mock and spy|mock is a full fake|spy wraps a real object|stub via when

sections.title: Five Test Doubles in Mockito
Choosing the Right Test Double
sections.content:
Use **Dummy** when a constructor or method requires a parameter you won't use in the test—mock it with no stubbing.

Use **Stub** when you need consistent fake data returned from a dependency, like a repository always returning the same Order object. This is 80% of Mockito usage.

Use **Fake** when the real implementation is too slow or complex but you need working logic—for example, an InMemoryUserRepository instead of PostgreSQL for integration tests.

Use **Mock** (with verify) when the test's purpose is confirming an interaction happened, like ensuring EmailService.send was called when an order completes.

Use **Spy** when testing a class where you want real methods to execute except for a few specific ones you need to control, like stubbing a slow API call in an otherwise fast service.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling everything a mock**: Freshers say "I'm mocking the repository" when they're actually stubbing it with when().thenReturn(). A true mock uses verify() to assert interactions. Imprecise language suggests unclear thinking about what the test validates.
- **Overusing verify()**: Writing verify() on every mock turns unit tests into fragile change detectors. Only verify interactions that matter to the test's purpose—if you're testing order totals, verifying that logger.info was called is noise.
- **Not knowing when to use Fakes**: Freshers mock everything when a simple Fake (like an in-memory list) would make tests clearer. If your test setup has ten when() statements recreating a repository's behavior, you need a Fake implementation instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Test Double**: generic term for any fake object replacing a real dependency in tests—not synonymous with mock
- **Dummy**: object passed to satisfy parameter requirements but never actually used in test execution
- **Stub**: returns pre-configured canned responses when called, most common pattern in Mockito with when().thenReturn()
- **Fake**: simplified working implementation with real logic but lighter infrastructure, like InMemoryRepository vs PostgreSQL
- **Mock**: records method calls and verifies interactions happened correctly using verify(), tests behavior not state
- **Spy**: wraps real object allowing most methods to execute normally while stubbing only specific ones
- **Gerard Meszaros**: author of xUnit Test Patterns who formalized these five test double types in 2007

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A test double is any fake object you use in place of a real dependency during testing. The term comes from Gerard Meszaros who defined five specific types in xUnit Test Patterns. Here's the breakdown. A Dummy is just a placeholder—you pass it to satisfy a parameter requirement but never actually use it in the test. A Stub returns canned data when called. Like if you stub a repository to always return the same Order object. That's what most people mean when they say mock, but technically they're stubbing. A Fake is a simplified working implementation. For example, an InMemoryOrderRepository that uses a Java list instead of hitting PostgreSQL. It has real logic but lighter infrastructure. A Mock is different—it records interactions and lets you verify they happened. So you'd use verify to check that EmailService dot send was called with the right arguments. Finally, a Spy wraps a real object. Most methods run the actual code, but you can stub specific ones. Like keeping all of a PaymentService's logic real except stubbing the slow fraud API call. The mistake freshers make is calling everything a mock when they're usually just stubbing. If you're not using verify, it's probably a stub not a mock. Understanding these distinctions shows you're thinking about testing strategy, not just tool syntax. When someone asks what you're testing—state or behavior—you'll know which double fits.

questions.question: How do you use doReturn().when() vs when().thenReturn() in Mockito?
questions.title: doReturn vs when thenReturn Mockito | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Both stub methods, but doReturn().when() avoids calling the real method during setup. For @Mock objects, both syntaxes work identically. For @Spy objects, when().thenReturn() calls the real method before stubbing it, which can trigger side effects or exceptions. Always use doReturn().when() with spies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's subtle API differences and when each syntax is appropriate for mocks vs spies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using when().thenReturn() on a @Spy and accidentally executing the real method during test setup, causing unexpected behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the execution sequence: when(spy.method()) invokes the real method to record the invocation before thenReturn applies the stub

sections.title: Two Stubbing Syntaxes in Mockito
sections.content:
Mockito provides two ways to stub method behavior: **when().thenReturn()** and **doReturn().when()**. At first glance they look like mirror images doing the same thing, and for **@Mock** objects they're functionally identical—use whichever reads better to you. But for **@Spy** objects, there's a critical difference that can break your tests. The when().thenReturn() syntax evaluates the method call inside when() to record what you're stubbing. For a spy, this means the real method actually executes during setup before the stub takes effect. If that real method throws an exception, queries a database, or has other side effects, your test fails or behaves unpredictably during setup, not during the actual test logic.

Think of it like setting up a stunt: when().thenReturn() makes the stunt double perform the dangerous jump once before filming so the director knows what to fake. doReturn().when() tells the director "just fake this jump" without any rehearsal. For mocks, the method is already fake so there's nothing to execute. For spies, you must use doReturn().when() to avoid triggering the real implementation during stubbing.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|when then return|~Readable, type-safe|default on mocks|calls real on spies|risky for spies
blue|do return when|~No real call|safe on spies|stubs void|skips the type check
emerald|The Rule|~Mocks use when|spies use do return|avoid spy side effects|same outcome

sections.title: when().thenReturn() vs doReturn().when()
sections.content:
| Aspect | when().thenReturn() | doReturn().when() |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax Style | BDD-style, reads naturally | Arrangement-style, more explicit |
| Method Invocation | Calls real method during stubbing | Never calls real method |
| With @Mock | Safe—method already fake | Safe—method already fake |
| With @Spy | Dangerous—real method executes | Safe—method not executed |
| Exception Handling | Real exceptions thrown during setup | No exceptions during setup |
| Type Safety | Compile-time checked return type | Return type checked at runtime |

sections.title: Syntax Difference with Spies
Choosing the Right Syntax
sections.content: Use **when().thenReturn()** for @Mock objects when you want natural BDD-style readability. It reads like English: "when this method is called, then return this value." Most Mockito examples use this syntax because it's intuitive. But always switch to **doReturn().when()** when working with @Spy objects. The moment you spy on a real object, the risk of unintended execution appears. Even if the real method seems harmless now, future changes might add side effects. As a safe rule: if you see @Spy, use doReturn().when(). Also use doReturn().when() when stubbing void methods or methods that throw exceptions, because the when() syntax doesn't work syntactically for those cases—you need doNothing().when() or doThrow().when() instead, which are the same family as doReturn().

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using when().thenReturn() with spies**: This is the number one mistake. Freshers copy-paste stubbing code from mock examples and apply it to spies. The real method runs during test setup, throws an exception or triggers a database call, and the test fails mysteriously before the actual test logic executes. Always grep for @Spy in your test class and verify you're using doReturn syntax.
- **Not understanding when() evaluates the call**: Freshers think when(spy.method()) is just syntax, not an actual method invocation. It's not magic—Java executes that method call to determine what you're stubbing. For spies, that means real code runs.
- **Inconsistent syntax mixing**: Using when().thenReturn() for some stubs and doReturn().when() for others in the same test without reason creates confusion. Pick doReturn consistently for spies, when consistently for mocks.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **when().thenReturn()**: BDD-style stubbing syntax that evaluates the method call inside when() to record the invocation
- **doReturn().when()**: arrangement-style syntax that stubs without invoking the real method, safer for spies
- **With @Mock**: both syntaxes functionally identical because no real method exists to invoke during stubbing
- **With @Spy**: when().thenReturn() calls the real method once during setup which can cause exceptions or side effects
- **Execution sequence**: when(spy.method()) actually runs spy's real method before thenReturn applies the stub
- **Safe rule**: always use doReturn().when() with @Spy to avoid unintended real method execution during test setup
- **Void methods**: doNothing().when() and doThrow().when() are required for void methods because when() syntax doesn't support them

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Both when dot thenReturn and doReturn dot when stub method behavior in Mockito, but there's a critical difference when you're working with spies. For at-Mock objects, they're identical—use whichever you prefer. The when syntax reads more naturally, like when repository dot findById is called then return this order. But for at-Spy objects, when dot thenReturn is dangerous. Here's why. When you write when spy dot checkFraud, Java actually executes that method call to figure out what you're stubbing. For a spy, that means the real checkFraud method runs during your test setup before the stub takes effect. If the real method throws an exception, queries a database, or has any side effects, your test fails or behaves unpredictably right there during setup, not during the actual test logic. With doReturn dot when, you never invoke the real method. You're telling Mockito directly which method to stub without executing it first. So the safe rule is: always use doReturn dot when with spies. Even if the real method seems harmless now, future code changes might add side effects. The mistake freshers make is copying stubbing code from mock examples and pasting it onto spies without realizing the difference. Their test mysteriously crashes during setup and they can't figure out why. The other place you need doReturn is stubbing void methods or methods that throw exceptions, because the when syntax doesn't support those cases syntactically. You'd use doNothing dot when or doThrow dot when instead. So bottom line: if you see at-Spy in your test, switch to the doReturn family of methods. It avoids accidental execution and keeps your test setup predictable.

questions.question: When would you use a Spy instead of a Mock?
questions.title: When to Use a Spy
questions.direct_answer: Use a Spy when you want the real methods of an object to execute by default, but you need to selectively stub or verify specific methods. This is useful for partial mocking scenarios like testing legacy code where most methods should run normally but you need to fake external dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spy enables partial mocking and when that's the right tool versus full isolation with Mock
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Spy as a default thinking it's more realistic, when most unit tests should use full Mocks for complete isolation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that doReturn().when() must be used with Spy to avoid calling the real method during stubbing setup

sections.title: Spy vs Mock: Partial vs Full Isolation
sections.content:
A **Spy** wraps a real object instance, calling actual methods by default unless you explicitly stub them. A **Mock** creates a hollow shell where every method returns default values (null, 0, false, empty collections) unless stubbed. Think of Spy as putting a transparent wrapper around a live object—you can intercept specific method calls while letting the rest pass through. Mock is more like building a cardboard cutout that only does what you explicitly tell it. Most unit tests should use Mocks for complete isolation from dependencies, but Spies shine when you're dealing with **legacy code** where refactoring is risky, or when you need to test one method of a class while letting other methods run their real implementation.

The key difference: Mocks isolate completely (you define all behavior), Spies delegate to real code (you override selectively).

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Use a Spy|~Mostly real behaviour|stub one method|legacy code|a partial mock
blue|Use a Mock|~Full isolation|no real code|the simplest default|most unit tests
emerald|Spy Caution|~Real methods run|use do return to stub|watch side effects|a smell if heavy

sections.title: Spy vs Mock in Action
Step 1: Does Your Test Need Real Business Logic?
sections.content: Ask yourself: do I need the actual implementation to run? If you're testing **OrderService** and it depends on **EmailService**, you probably don't want real emails sent—use a **Mock**. But if you're testing **CompositeValidator** that chains multiple validation rules, and you only want to fake one external API call inside one validator, use a **Spy** on the whole validator and stub just that problematic method. Rule of thumb: if you need zero real behavior from a dependency, Mock it. If you need most methods to work normally but want to intercept a few, Spy it. Spies are common in integration tests where you want to keep most of the application stack running but replace a single external call like a third-party HTTP client.

sections.title: Step 2: Can You Refactor Instead of Using Spy?
sections.content: Before reaching for a Spy, consider if your design could be improved. If you're spying on a class because you can't cleanly mock its dependencies, that's a **code smell**—the class might be doing too much or have hard-coded dependencies. Extract the problematic behavior into an interface you can mock. Spies are often a pragmatic choice for **legacy code** where refactoring is too risky or time-consuming, but for new code, they usually signal that you haven't properly separated concerns. If you find yourself stubbing more than 1-2 methods on a Spy, you probably should be using a full Mock or refactoring the class. Spies are a tool for specific situations, not a default choice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using when().thenReturn() with Spy**: Freshers write when(spy.method()).thenReturn(value) which actually calls the real method during setup, potentially causing errors. With Spies, always use doReturn(value).when(spy).method() to avoid calling the real implementation during stubbing.
- **Overusing Spies in unit tests**: Thinking Spies are more realistic so using them everywhere, but this defeats the purpose of unit testing—fast, isolated tests. Spies are slower because real code runs, and they couple your tests to implementation details.
- **Not initializing the Spy with a real object**: Writing @Spy private Service service; without initializing it. Spies need a real instance, either via @Spy private Service service = new Service(); or by letting Mockito inject dependencies with @InjectMocks.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spy wraps real object**: unstubbed methods execute actual implementation, unlike Mock where all methods return defaults
- **Use doReturn().when() syntax**: avoid when().thenReturn() with Spies because it calls the real method during setup
- **Partial mocking use case**: Spy is for scenarios where you need most real behavior but want to fake specific methods
- **Legacy code tool**: Spies are most useful when testing hard-to-refactor legacy code where dependencies are baked in
- **Performance consideration**: Spies run real code so tests are slower than using full Mocks for isolation
- **Verification works on both**: you can verify() method calls on Spies just like Mocks, even for unstubbed methods
- **Design smell indicator**: frequent need for Spies in new code suggests classes have too many responsibilities or tight coupling

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd use a Spy instead of a Mock when I need most of a class's methods to run their real implementation, but I want to stub or verify just a few specific methods. The classic example is testing legacy code where you can't easily inject dependencies—maybe you have a service class with ten methods and nine of them work fine, but one calls an external API you don't want to hit in tests. With a Spy, those nine methods run normally while you stub out the API call. The key difference from a Mock is that Mock returns null or empty values for everything unless you stub it, while Spy calls the actual code unless you override it. One important gotcha—you have to use the doReturn-when syntax with Spies, not the regular when-thenReturn, because when-thenReturn actually calls the real method to set up the stub, which can cause problems. In practice, I'd prefer Mocks for most unit tests because they give you complete isolation and are faster, but Spies are really useful for integration-style tests where you want to keep most of the real stack running. If I find myself needing a Spy in new code though, I'd step back and consider whether the class needs refactoring—maybe I can extract that problematic dependency into an interface I can mock cleanly instead.

questions.question: What is a Fake object and how does it differ from a Mock?
questions.title: Fake Object vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: A Fake is a working implementation with simplified logic used for testing, like an H2 in-memory database or a HashMap-backed repository. A Mock is a framework-generated test double that verifies method calls and returns stubbed values. Fakes have real behavior; Mocks have expectation-based verification.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the broader test double vocabulary beyond what Mockito provides and when to write custom Fakes instead of using mocking frameworks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Fakes with Mocks because both are test objects, missing that Fakes implement real logic while Mocks only verify interactions without actual business logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete examples like H2 for database Fakes or writing a simple in-memory fake repository class for tests, and explain when Fakes are better than Mocks

sections.title: Fakes Have Real Logic, Mocks Have Expectations
sections.content:
A **Fake** is a lightweight, working implementation you write specifically for testing—it has actual business logic, just simplified. Think of an **H2 in-memory database** replacing PostgreSQL, or a **HashMap-based repository** instead of JPA.

The Fake's methods do real work: they store data, perform calculations, return computed results. A **Mock** is a test double generated by Mockito that has no real logic—it's just a recording device that remembers what methods were called and returns pre-programmed stub values. Mocks verify interactions (was this method called with these arguments?), while Fakes verify behavior through their real implementation. The mental model: if you're checking whether methodX was called, you're using a Mock. If you're checking that data was stored correctly and can be retrieved, you're using a Fake. Fakes bridge the gap between unit and integration tests—they let you test real workflows without slow external dependencies.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Fake|~A light implementation|an in-memory map|real logic, simplified|stateful
blue|Mock|~A programmed fake|returns set values|verifies calls|no real logic
emerald|Pick Rule|~Fake for stateful deps|an in-memory repo|mock for boundaries|external systems

sections.title: Fake Repository vs Mocked Repository
When to Choose Fake vs Mock
sections.content:
Use a **Fake** when you need to test workflows that depend on stateful behavior or complex interactions across multiple calls—like saving an order then retrieving it, or testing a cache implementation. Fakes work great for **data access layers** (in-memory repository instead of database), **external APIs** (fake payment gateway that approves test transactions), or **file systems** (HashMap instead of disk).

Use a **Mock** when you just need to verify a method was called with correct parameters, especially for **stateless services** or **external integrations** you don't control. If your test is checking that EmailService.send() was called when an order completes, Mock it. If you're testing that UserService correctly handles duplicate email registrations across multiple operations, a Fake repository makes the test clearer and more reliable than stubbing multiple find/save calls.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating Fakes as production code**: Writing overly complex Fakes that replicate all production logic including error handling and edge cases. Fakes should be intentionally simplified—just enough to support your test scenarios. If your Fake is more than 50 lines, you're probably overdoing it.
- **Using Mocks when Fakes would be clearer**: Stubbing ten different method calls on a mocked repository when a simple FakeRepository with a HashMap would make the test's intent obvious. Over-mocking creates brittle tests that break when implementation changes.
- **Not sharing Fakes across tests**: Writing the same FakeUserRepository in every test class. Create one Fake per interface in a shared test utilities package and reuse it—this is one case where test code duplication is actually worse than sharing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fake has real logic**: it's a lightweight working implementation you write, not a framework-generated double
- **Mock has no logic**: Mockito Mocks just record calls and return stubbed values, no actual behavior
- **H2 is a Fake**: in-memory databases, HashMap repositories, and test payment gateways are classic Fake examples
- **Fakes enable state testing**: you can save data in a Fake and retrieve it later, Mocks can't maintain state naturally
- **Mocks verify interactions**: use verify() to check method calls, Fakes verify through their actual behavior
- **Fakes reduce stubbing**: one Fake replaces dozens of when-thenReturn statements for stateful scenarios
- **Martin Fowler terminology**: Fake is one of five test doubles (Dummy, Stub, Spy, Mock, Fake) defined in testing literature

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A Fake is a real working implementation that you write yourself for testing purposes—it has actual business logic, just simplified. The classic example is using H2, an in-memory database, instead of PostgreSQL in tests. H2 is a Fake because it actually stores data and runs SQL queries, just faster and in memory. Another common Fake is a HashMap-backed repository—it really saves and retrieves data, just using a map instead of a database. A Mock is totally different. It's generated by Mockito and has zero business logic—it just remembers what methods were called and returns whatever values you programmed with when-thenReturn. You use Mocks to verify interactions, like checking that sendEmail was called with the right parameters. You use Fakes to test actual workflows, like saving a user then looking them up by ID. The key difference is Fakes do real work with simplified logic, while Mocks just record and playback. In practice, I'd use a Fake when I need stateful behavior across multiple method calls—like testing that my service correctly handles duplicate registrations by checking the repository. I'd use a Mock for simple one-off verifications like making sure an external API got called. Fakes take more effort to write but they make complex tests way more readable and maintainable than stubbing twenty different method calls on a Mock.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpyBean and @MockBean in a Spring Boot test?
questions.title: @SpyBean vs @MockBean in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @MockBean replaces a Spring bean in the application context with a full Mockito mock where all methods return defaults. @SpyBean wraps the real Spring bean instance so unstubbed methods run the actual implementation. Both dirty the Spring context, forcing a reload for each test class that uses them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring Boot test annotations and their integration with Mockito, plus understanding of application context lifecycle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean when only one method needs stubbing, causing unnecessary full mocking and context reloads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that both annotations dirty the Spring context, causing performance degradation in large test suites, and suggest @MockBean for external dependencies only

sections.title: Spring Context Integration: Full Replacement vs Partial Wrapping
sections.content:
Both **@MockBean** and **@SpyBean** are Spring Boot test annotations that integrate Mockito with the Spring application context, but they differ fundamentally in what they replace. **@MockBean** removes the real bean from the context and injects a pure Mockito mock—all methods return null, 0, false, or empty collections unless you stub them. **@SpyBean** keeps the real bean instance but wraps it in a Mockito spy, so unstubbed methods execute actual code. The critical performance impact: both annotations **dirty the Spring context**, meaning Spring must reload the entire application context for each test class using them.

If TestClassA uses @MockBean for ServiceX and TestClassB mocks ServiceY, Spring creates two separate contexts, doubling startup time. This is why you should minimize their use and never mix different @MockBean configurations across test classes—it multiplies context reloads exponentially.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the MockBean annotation|~A full fake bean|replaces it in context|methods stubbed|return defaults
blue|the SpyBean annotation|~A real bean wrapped|real methods run|stub selectively|partial
emerald|When|~MockBean to isolate|SpyBean to keep real|verify on either|Spring context needed

sections.title: Code Example
MockBean vs SpyBean Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @MockBean | @SpyBean |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bean Replacement | Completely replaces bean with mock | Wraps real bean instance |
| Unstubbed Methods | Return defaults (null, 0, false) | Execute actual implementation |
| Primary Use Case | External dependencies (APIs, DB) | Partial mocking of Spring beans |
| Context Impact | Dirties context, forces reload | Dirties context, forces reload |
| Typical Target | Feign clients, repositories, external services | Internal services with mostly real logic |

sections.title: When to Choose Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@MockBean** for external dependencies you don't want to run in tests: third-party API clients (Feign, RestTemplate), message queues, external authentication services. These should be completely mocked because you want zero real interaction. Also use @MockBean when you need every method of a bean stubbed—if you're replacing behavior wholesale, full mocking is clearer.

Use **@SpyBean** when you need most of a Spring bean's real methods to run but want to stub one or two specific methods—like testing an OrderService that depends on EmailService, and you want the real order processing logic but need to fake the email sending. However, consider whether you even need Spring context for your test. If you're testing one service with mocked dependencies, use plain @Mock with @InjectMocks instead—way faster, no context reload penalty.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Overusing @MockBean everywhere**: Freshers add @MockBean to every dependency, not realizing each combination of mocked beans creates a new Spring context. In a 100-test suite, this can add minutes to test runtime. Only mock what you absolutely need, and try to use the same @MockBean configuration across related test classes.
- **Using @SpyBean for external services**: Spying on a real database repository or HTTP client defeats the purpose—you want isolation, not partially real external calls. Spy internal business logic, mock external integrations.
- **Not understanding context caching**: Writing @MockBean UserService in ClassA and @MockBean OrderService in ClassB, not realizing Spring now loads two contexts. Group related mocks in an abstract base test class so multiple test classes share one context configuration.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@MockBean replaces completely**: removes real bean from Spring context and injects a full Mockito mock
- **@SpyBean wraps real bean**: keeps actual instance but allows selective stubbing and verification
- **Both dirty context**: each unique combination of mock beans forces Spring to create a new application context
- **Performance cost**: context reloads add significant time to test suites, minimize use of these annotations
- **External vs internal**: use @MockBean for external dependencies, @SpyBean for internal services with partial mocking needs
- **Alternative exists**: consider plain @Mock with @InjectMocks for unit tests, avoid Spring context overhead when possible
- **Test slices help**: @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest load only relevant beans, reducing context size and reload cost

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference is what they do to the Spring bean. At-MockBean completely replaces a bean in the Spring application context with a Mockito mock—every method returns null or default values unless you stub it. At-SpyBean wraps the real Spring bean so unstubbed methods still run the actual implementation. So if I have a UserService bean and I use at-MockBean, calling any method without stubbing returns null. But with at-SpyBean, those methods actually execute the real UserService code. The critical thing that catches freshers off guard is both of them dirty the Spring context. That means if TestClassA uses at-MockBean for ServiceX and TestClassB uses at-MockBean for ServiceY, Spring has to reload the entire application context twice—once for each test class. This can make test suites really slow. I'd use at-MockBean for external dependencies like Feign clients or repositories when I want complete isolation and don't want any real external calls. I'd use at-SpyBean when I need most of a Spring bean's real behavior but want to fake one specific method, though honestly this is pretty rare—it often signals the class is doing too much. In practice, for most unit tests I'd avoid both and just use plain at-Mock with at-InjectMocks because it's way faster without the Spring context overhead. Reserve at-MockBean for integration tests where you genuinely need the Spring context but want to replace external dependencies.

questions.question: Can you spy on a final class or a static method in Mockito, and how?
questions.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
questions.direct_answer: Yes, Mockito 2.x introduced the inline mock maker that can mock final classes and methods, and since Mockito 3.4.0 you can use mockStatic() to stub static methods. However, heavy reliance on these features often indicates design problems—prefer refactoring to use dependency injection or wrapper classes instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Mockito's extended capabilities beyond basic mocking and the design implications of needing these advanced features
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Mockito can never mock final or static, missing the inline mock maker feature introduced in Mockito 2.x, or over-relying on these features instead of fixing design
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that while technically possible with mockito-inline artifact, mocking statics is often a code smell signaling tight coupling, suggest dependency injection or wrapper patterns as better solutions

sections.title: Extended Mocking Capabilities with Trade-offs
sections.content:
Modern Mockito can mock **final classes**, **final methods**, and even **static methods**, capabilities that were impossible in earlier versions. Mockito 2.x introduced the **inline mock maker** which uses bytecode manipulation to handle final types, and Mockito 3.4.0+ added **mockStatic()** for static method stubbing.

To enable final class mocking, Mockito automatically uses the inline mock maker if it detects the **mockito-inline** artifact on your classpath. For static methods, you explicitly call mockStatic(ClassName.class) which returns a scoped mock you must close after use. However, here's the critical insight: if you frequently need to mock finals or statics, it's usually a **design smell**. Final classes and static methods are hard to test because they represent tight coupling—code that directly depends on concrete implementations rather than abstractions. The better fix is usually refactoring: extract an interface, use dependency injection, or wrap static calls in an injected service.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Old Limitation|~Final and static|once unsupported|needed PowerMock|a proxy-based engine
blue|Modern Mockito|~Now supported|mockito-inline|mockStatic|spy final classes
emerald|Advice|~Prefer a redesign|inject dependencies|avoid static calls|inline as a last resort

sections.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
When These Features Are Justified
sections.content:
**Legacy code scenarios**: You're adding tests to existing code where refactoring is too risky or expensive. The class is final because the original developer didn't consider testability. Static method mocking is acceptable here as a pragmatic compromise.

**Third-party final classes**: Libraries that ship final classes without interfaces (though most well-designed libraries avoid this). You can't change their code, so mocking is your only option.

**Time/random testing**: Mocking LocalDateTime.now() or Math.random() for deterministic tests is a legitimate use case—these are utility statics where the alternative (injecting a Clock or RandomGenerator) adds ceremony. However, if you're writing **new code** and reaching for these features, stop and refactor. Extract interfaces, use constructor injection, wrap static utilities in services. The pain of mocking finals/statics is a signal that your design has tight coupling that will cause maintenance problems beyond just testing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not closing mockStatic scope**: Writing mockStatic(Class.class) without try-with-resources, causing the static mock to leak into other tests and creating bizarre failures. Static mocks MUST be closed, preferably using try-with-resources to guarantee cleanup.
- **Using static mocking as default**: Freshers discover mockStatic() and start using it everywhere instead of fixing design. If you're mocking static utility classes in every test, extract those utilities into an injected service bean.
- **Missing mockito-inline dependency**: Trying to mock a final class and getting a MockitoException that final types can't be mocked. You need the mockito-inline artifact explicitly added to your test dependencies—gradle: testImplementation 'org.mockito:mockito-inline:5.x.x' or Maven equivalent.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Inline mock maker**: Mockito 2.x+ can mock final classes and methods using bytecode instrumentation via mockito-inline artifact
- **mockStatic() for statics**: Mockito 3.4.0+ provides mockStatic(Class.class) that returns a scoped mock requiring explicit closure
- **Try-with-resources required**: static mocks must be closed to avoid leaking into other tests, use try-with-resources pattern
- **Design smell indicator**: frequent need to mock finals or statics suggests tight coupling and poor separation of concerns
- **Refactoring is better**: extract interfaces, use dependency injection, or wrap static utilities in injectable service classes
- **Legacy code exception**: mocking finals/statics is justified for adding tests to existing hard-to-refactor code
- **Performance cost**: inline mock maker uses bytecode manipulation which is slower than standard mocking, use sparingly

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Yes, you can mock both final classes and static methods in modern Mockito, but there are some important caveats. For final classes, Mockito 2.x introduced the inline mock maker that uses bytecode instrumentation to create mocks of final types. You just need the mockito-inline artifact in your test dependencies, and then you can mock final classes exactly like regular classes—Mockito handles it automatically. For static methods, Mockito 3.4.0 added the mockStatic method that creates a scoped mock of static calls. You call mockStatic with the class, stub your methods, but critically you must close the mock when done, usually with try-with-resources. If you don't close it, the static mock leaks into other tests and causes weird failures. Now here's the important part that shows deeper understanding: if you're frequently needing these features in new code, it's usually a design smell. Final classes and static methods are hard to test because they represent tight coupling—your code depends directly on concrete implementations. The better solution is refactoring: extract an interface you can implement and inject, or wrap static utility calls in a service class. Static mocking is fine for things like LocalDateTime.now when you need deterministic time in tests, but if you're mocking business logic statics, that's a signal to use dependency injection instead. These features exist mainly for dealing with legacy code or third-party libraries where you can't change the design.
